exploreAction.targetName: White on White (1918) — the zero of painting
exploreAction.instruction: Give it a full minute: a white square floats on a white field, and the only thing to look at is the difference — the tilt, the brushstrokes, the faint seam where one white meets another. Malevich called this the final painting of art: after the black square came the red, and then this, the zero point where color disappears and only space and feeling remain.

name: Twittering Machine (1922)
teaser: Four birds perch on a wire cranked by a hand wheel — a little machine for making birdsong, drawn in a few wiry lines. But the joke is darker than it looks: the birds are trapped, the crank is the handle of a birdcatcher's device, and the song they 'twitter' is a snare. Klee's tiny, poisonous cartoon is one of the most reproduced images in modern art.

exploreAction.targetName: Twittering Machine (1922) — the birds and the crank
exploreAction.instruction: Work the crank in your head: a hand wheel turns a wire on which four birds stand, their beaks open — they are twittering, but the machine is a snare, and the handle is there to turn the trap. Klee built the whole thing from a few wiry lines, ink and watercolor, and the lightness hides the cruelty: the birds sing because they cannot fly away.

name: Senecio (1922)
teaser: A face built from geometric planes — a mask with segmented forehead, cheeks, and eyes, one brow arched, the colors glowing against a deep background. 'Senecio' is Latin for 'old man,' and Klee built the head from the same language of squares and triangles he taught at the Bauhaus: a portrait reduced to architecture, both playful and unsettling.

exploreAction.targetName: Senecio (1922) — the geometric mask
exploreAction.instruction: Read the face as a building: forehead, cheeks, and chin are separate colored planes — orange, red, ochre — fitted together like masonry, with two dark eyes and one raised eyebrow giving it a sly, ancient expression. Klee taught color theory at the Bauhaus when he painted this, and the head is a demonstration: a portrait built from pure geometry, half mask, half old man. The circles and angles hover between cartoon and icon.

name: Puberty (1894-95)
teaser: A naked adolescent girl sits on the edge of a bed, hands clasped in her lap, staring straight at us while a great dark shadow looms behind her. Painted over and over by Munch, who was haunted by the moment childhood ends. The shadow is everything she is about to become — sexuality, anxiety, the adult world — and the painting made Munch notorious.

exploreAction.targetName: Puberty (1894-95) — the girl and the shadow
exploreAction.instruction: Meet her stare: a girl on the edge of a bed, naked, hands clasped in her lap, looks straight at you with a gaze that is half defiance and half terror — while behind her a dark mass rises like a door opening. Munch painted this subject repeatedly, obsessed with the instant childhood ends. The bed, the sheets, the shadow: every element is stripped to its simplest form, and the painting's power is that nothing is explained.

name: Vampire (1893-94)
teaser: A woman with flowing red hair bends over a man, her lips pressed to his neck — originally titled 'Love and Pain,' renamed 'Vampire' by a friend, and it stuck. The red hair pours down like blood, the embrace is both comfort and consumption, and Munch painted six versions. Love as a wound: the most tender horror painting ever made.

exploreAction.targetName: Vampire (1893-94) — the red hair and the kiss
exploreAction.instruction: Find the blood before the kiss: the woman's red hair pours down over the man's shoulders and neck like a wound, and her face against his skin is both an embrace and a bite. Munch titled it 'Love and Pain'; a friend renamed it 'Vampire,' and the new title won. He painted six versions over twenty years, and the image keeps its ambiguity — is she comforting him or feeding?

name: Portrait of Wally (1912)
teaser: Wally Neuzil, Schiele's lover and model — they met when she was seventeen, and he painted her with an unflinching directness that shocked Vienna: pale skin, dark circles, a gaze that holds nothing back. Schiele later left her for his wife; Wally died of scarlet fever in 1917, and Schiele died of Spanish flu the next year. The painting was looted by Nazis and spent a decade in a famous restitution battle.

exploreAction.targetName: Portrait of Wally (1912) — the unflinching gaze
exploreAction.instruction: Hold her gaze: Wally Neuzil was seventeen when she became Schiele's model and lover, and he painted her with a directness Vienna found scandalous — the pale face, the dark eyes, the bare shoulder against the dark ground. Schiele left her to marry another woman; she died of scarlet fever in 1917 and he died of Spanish flu the next year.

name: Judith and the Head of Holofernes (1901)
teaser: Klimt's Judith — gold, bare-shouldered, eyes half-closed with triumph — holds the severed head of Holofernes at arm's length. Vienna immediately mistook her for Salome, the femme fatale; Klimt insisted she was Judith, the biblical heroine. The gold-leaf background and the erotic charge made it the sensation of the Secession, and the painting still reads as a portrait of feminine power wearing its victory like jewelry.

exploreAction.targetName: Judith and the Head of Holofernes (1901) — the gold and the head
exploreAction.instruction: Look at her face before the head: eyes half-closed, lips parted, a gold collar tight at her throat — she looks not triumphant but intoxicated, holding the severed head as if it were a handbag. Vienna assumed she was Salome; Klimt insisted she was Judith, the widow who saved her people. The gold leaf is hammered into the background like jewelry, her bare shoulder gleams, and the head is painted with a grim realism that makes the fantasy bite.

name: The Tree of Life (Stoclet Frieze) (1909)
teaser: Klimt's only major architectural commission outside Vienna: a mosaic frieze for a Brussels mansion, its center a great spiraling tree with gold branches — black trunks twisting into curls of gold and enamel, with a standing female figure and a pair embracing in the side panels. The swirl of the tree has been borrowed by a thousand designers; it is Klimt's cosmos as a garden.

exploreAction.targetName: The Tree of Life (Stoclet Frieze) (1909) — the golden spiral
exploreAction.instruction: Follow one spiral and get lost: the tree's trunk twists into curling gold branches that never quite repeat, an abstract forest of enamel, gold, and semiprecious stone that Klimt designed for a Brussels dining room in 1909. It is his cosmos as a garden — the spirals suggesting growth, time, and eternity. On the left a woman stands in a jeweled dress; on the right a couple embraces in a shower of gold.

name: Dream Caused by the Flight of a Bee Around a Pomegranate a Second Before Awakening (1944)
teaser: Dalí's chain-reaction dream: a sleeping Gala floats above a rock; from a pomegranate bursts a fish, from the fish's mouth two tigers and a rifle with a bayonet — all triggered, Dalí explained, by the sound of a bee, the way a single sting can ignite a whole dream. Painted for a dream sequence in a Hitchcock film that was never made, it is Surrealism as an equation.

exploreAction.targetName: The flight of a bee dream (1944) — the chain reaction
exploreAction.instruction: Read it as a chain reaction: the bee (tiny, lower left) stings, and the sound detonates the dream — pomegranate, fish, tigers, rifle, all exploding from one another in sequence, while Gala sleeps suspended above the sea. Dalí said the image was the literal illustration of a dream mechanism: one sensory jolt, and the mind builds a narrative. He painted it for a Hitchcock dream sequence that was cut from the film, so the dream survives only here.

name: Galatea of the Spheres (1952)
teaser: Gala's face built entirely from spheres — thousands of painted balls of color that only assemble into a portrait from a distance. Painted in Dalí's 'nuclear mysticism' period, after Hiroshima, when he was trying to paint matter as particles and the atom as the new holy image. Stand close and it is dots; step back and it is his wife's face.

exploreAction.targetName: Galatea of the Spheres (1952) — the face of particles
exploreAction.instruction: Do the experiment the painting demands: stand close and it is thousands of colored spheres — particles of paint, no face at all. Step back and the spheres assemble into Gala, his wife's face, floating in a space that looks like an atomic diagram. Dalí painted this after Hiroshima, in his 'nuclear mysticism' phase, when he believed matter itself was the new sacred image.

name: Self-Portrait with Cropped Hair (1940)
teaser: After divorcing Diego Rivera, Frida cut off her long hair, dressed in an oversized man's suit, and painted herself holding the scissors — strands of severed hair scattered around her. The lyrics at the top, from a Mexican song, say: 'Look, if I loved you it was because of your hair; now that you're bald, I don't love you anymore.' Defiance, grief, and reinvention in one canvas.

exploreAction.targetName: Self-Portrait with Cropped Hair (1940) — the scissors and the suit
exploreAction.instruction: Read the lyrics she wrote across the top: 'Look, if I loved you it was because of your hair; now that you're bald, I don't love you anymore' — a Mexican song, painted by Frida right after her divorce from Diego Rivera. She sits in an oversized man's suit, scissors in one hand, the shorn hair scattered in dark snakes around the chair.

name: Viva la Vida, Watermelons (1954)
teaser: Kahlo's last painting — watermelons, the Mexican fruit of the Day of the Dead, split open to show their red flesh, painted days before she died at 47. She signed it with her name, the date, and 'Viva la Vida' — long live life — across the red heart of the melons. A still life that is also a farewell, full of the taste and color of Mexico.

exploreAction.targetName: Viva la Vida, Watermelons (1954) — the last melons
exploreAction.instruction: Notice what she signed: 'Viva la Vida — Frida Kahlo, 1954, Coyoacán' written across the red flesh of a cut watermelon, the Mexican fruit of the Day of the Dead. It was painted days before she died at 47, and it is a goodbye that refuses to be sad: the melons are split open, glowing red, seed-spattered, alive.

name: Man at the Crossroads (1934)
teaser: Rivera's mural for Rockefeller Center in New York — a worker at the center of a wheel of modern life, with telescopes, factories, and a portrait of Lenin. Nelson Rockefeller asked Rivera to remove Lenin; Rivera refused, and the mural was destroyed in 1934. Rivera recreated it the next year in Mexico City as 'Man, Controller of the Universe.' The most famous destroyed painting of the 20th century.

exploreAction.targetName: Man at the Crossroads (1934) — the mural Rockefeller destroyed
exploreAction.instruction: Stand at the center with the worker: the mural was a giant wheel of modern life for Rockefeller Center — telescopes, machines, crowds — and at its heart Rivera painted Lenin, which is why Nelson Rockefeller ordered it destroyed.

name: Black Iris (1926)
teaser: An iris blown up until it fills the whole canvas — dark velvet petals, a black heart, a flower the size of a landscape. Critics immediately read it as anatomy; O'Keeffe spent decades denying it. She said she painted flowers large because 'nobody sees a flower — really — it is so small,' and her big flowers made her the most famous woman artist in America.

exploreAction.targetName: Black Iris (1926) — the flower as landscape
exploreAction.instruction: Get close enough that the flower becomes a landscape: O'Keefe enlarged this iris until its dark petals fill the canvas and its center becomes a black, velvet tunnel. She said she painted flowers big because nobody really sees a flower — it is so small — and the scale turns the petal into a mountain. The public insisted it was a portrait of a woman's body; she insisted it was a flower, and the argument is half the painting's life.

name: Automat (1927)
teaser: A woman sits alone at a window in a coin-operated cafeteria at night, a cup of coffee before her, the black window behind her — one of the great images of urban loneliness. Hopper's wife Jo posed for it. The automat, where city workers ate alone in the glow of electric light, was the perfect stage for his favorite subject: people together in public, alone in private.

exploreAction.targetName: Automat (1927) — the black window and the coffee
exploreAction.instruction: Notice the window does the work: it is a black rectangle, not a view — the night outside is just darkness, so the woman's isolation is doubled, reflected in glass she can't see through. Hopper's wife Jo posed for this, sitting alone in an automat, the coin-operated cafeteria where the city ate without speaking.

name: House by the Railroad (1925)
teaser: A lonely Victorian house stands beside an empty railroad track, cut off at the bottom of the canvas — Hopper's first great mature painting, and the image that made his name. The house has no people, no motion, no warmth; the tracks are empty; the sky is flat. Hitchcock's art director copied it directly for the Bates house in Psycho.

exploreAction.targetName: House by the Railroad (1925) — the house that became Psycho's
exploreAction.instruction: Let the house stare back: a Victorian mansion stands alone above an empty railroad track, cropped at the bottom of the frame like a photograph, and nothing in it moves. Hopper painted this in 1925 and it made him famous — the architecture of loneliness, a house that looks lived-out. The tracks are empty, the sky is flat, no people, no weather.

name: Freedom from Want (1943)
teaser: The Thanksgiving painting: a family around a table as the grandmother sets down the turkey, and everyone turns to face us. It is one of Rockwell's Four Freedoms, inspired by Roosevelt's 1941 speech, and the series sold $132 million in war bonds. The grandmother is Rockwell's real cook; the turkey took days to paint and the whole table is a portrait of a nation's self-image.

exploreAction.targetName: Freedom from Want (1943) — the Thanksgiving table
exploreAction.instruction: Count the faces turned to you: every person at the table looks out at the viewer, not at the turkey — Rockwell's grandmother (actually his cook) is placing the bird, and the scene is less a dinner than a declaration. Painted in 1943 as one of the Four Freedoms after Roosevelt's speech, it became the most reproduced American image of its decade and helped sell $132 million in war bonds.

name: The Problem We All Live With (1964)
teaser: Six-year-old Ruby Bridges walks to school in New Orleans escorted by four federal marshals, past a wall scrawled with racial slurs and a smashed tomato at her feet — Rockwell's first major civil-rights painting, published in Look magazine in 1964. Ruby, the first Black child to integrate her school, grew up to meet President Obama at the White House, where the painting now hangs.

exploreAction.targetName: The Problem We All Live With (1964) — Ruby's walk to school
exploreAction.instruction: Walk with the smallest figure in American civil-rights art: six-year-old Ruby Bridges, in a white dress, carrying her books, flanked by four faceless federal marshals. The wall behind her carries the word no one in the painting says aloud, and a tomato has splattered at her feet. Rockwell, known for warm humor, painted this in 1964 for Look magazine, and it was his first major statement on race.

name: In the Car (1963)
teaser: A couple in a convertible — the woman crying, the man staring ahead — blown up from a comic-book panel with Ben-Day dots and a speech bubble that says 'I don't care! I'd rather sink — than call Brad for help!' Lichtenstein took melodrama from the funnies and made it monumental, and the dots are the point: the artificial made honest.

exploreAction.targetName: In the Car (1963) — the dots and the drama
exploreAction.instruction: Read the bubble out loud: 'I don't care! I'd rather sink — than call Brad for help!' — comic-book melodrama, blown up to a wall-sized canvas with the Ben-Day dots you can count from two feet away. Lichtenstein copied the panel from an actual comic and made the artificiality the subject: the dots, the primary colors, the frozen drama.

name: Flowers (1964)
teaser: Warhol's flowers — silk-screened hibiscus blooms cropped from a magazine photograph, repeated in candy colors across a green background. Made in his Factory, mass-produced like cans of soup, they were shown at the 1964 Venice Biennale as a suite. The flowers are pure surface: cheerful, decorative, and completely deadpan — nature turned into product.

exploreAction.targetName: Flowers (1964) — the factory blooms
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the surface and ask where the feeling went: these flowers were cropped from a photography magazine, silk-screened by Factory assistants, and repeated in candy colors — hibiscus blooms as standardized as soup cans. The green background is a single flat field, the flowers have no stems or context, and each print is slightly misregistered, the silk-screen wobble showing through.

name: Race Riot (1964)
teaser: Warhol's first political series: a Life magazine photo of Birmingham police dogs attacking a Black protester, repeated in harsh reds and blues. He was 'surprised' people were shocked, he said — he thought it was 'just a picture.' The repetition drains and sharpens the violence at once: the image is everywhere and nowhere, and the painting refuses to let you look away or look once.

exploreAction.targetName: Race Riot (1964) — the dogs and the repetition
exploreAction.instruction: Feel the repetition do the violence: Warhol took one photo — police dogs attacking a Black protester in Birmingham — and printed it again and again in brutal red and blue, the image wobbling out of register like a damaged newspaper.

name: Bed (1955)
teaser: A real quilt and pillow, stretched on a wooden frame and slashed with paint — Rauschenberg's own bed, hung on the wall as the first 'combine' between painting and sculpture. He was broke, he said, so the bed was the only canvas he had. The paint runs down the quilt like blood or like the stains of living, and the piece sits somewhere between painting, collage, and confession.

exploreAction.targetName: Bed (1955) — the quilt as canvas
exploreAction.instruction: Touch the history under the paint: this is Rauschenberg's actual bed — the quilt, the pillow, the sheet — hung vertically and covered with paint that drips and smears like a crime scene or a night of living. He called it a 'combine,' part painting, part sculpture, made in 1955 when he was too broke to buy canvas, so he used what he had.

name: Painted Bronze (1960)
teaser: Two bronze objects cast from real things and painted to look real: a Savarin coffee can stuffed with brushes, and a pair of Ballantine ale cans. Johns made the ale cans after Willem de Kooning complained about a gallery owner, and the story goes a friend said 'if you make it, you can't buy it' — so he did. Bronze pretending to be tin: a joke about art, money, and seeing.

exploreAction.targetName: Painted Bronze (1960) — the bronze ale cans
exploreAction.instruction: Wait for the moment of double take: these look like a coffee can of brushes and two ale cans, but they are bronze — cast from the real objects and painted by hand to fool your eye. Jasper Johns made them around 1960, reportedly after a remark that if he made the cans himself he couldn't be charged gallery prices for them.

name: Woman I (1952)
teaser: De Kooning's Woman — painted, scraped, and repainted for two years, a figure built from furious strokes: huge eyes, toothy grin, body carved out of slabs of color. Critics called it a portrait of misogyny; de Kooning called it 'a woman,' grinning and monstrous and alive. It is the most fought-over painting of Abstract Expressionism: the human figure refusing to disappear from abstract art.

exploreAction.targetName: Woman I (1952) — the woman who wouldn't leave
exploreAction.instruction: Feel the fight in the paint: de Kooning worked on this one canvas for two years, painting it out and starting over until the surface is a battlefield of scraped and repainted layers. The woman is all contradictions — enormous eyes, a grin that is either welcoming or devouring, a body built from slabs of color that never quite resolve.

name: Full Fathom Five (1947)
teaser: One of Pollock's first great drip paintings — and hidden in the web of paint are real objects: coins, nails, buttons, cigarettes, matches, a paint tube, embedded in the surface like fossils. The title comes from Shakespeare's The Tempest ('Full fathom five thy father lies'), and the canvas is a portrait of the studio floor: everything that fell into the picture stayed.

exploreAction.targetName: Full Fathom Five (1947) — the buried coins and nails
exploreAction.instruction: Hunt for the buried objects: this is one of Pollock's first mature drip paintings, and pressed into the black and silver web are real things — coins, nails, buttons, cigarettes, matches — that fell in as he worked and were sealed there forever.

name: Mountains and Sea (1952)
teaser: Frankenthaler, 23 years old, poured thinned paint onto raw, unprimed canvas so the color sank into the fiber instead of sitting on top — the 'soak-stain' method that birthed Color Field painting. The result looks like a watercolor the size of a wall: mountains and sea dissolving into each other. Morris Louis and Kenneth Noland came to her studio, saw it, and changed their art overnight.

exploreAction.targetName: Mountains and Sea (1952) — the stain that started a movement
exploreAction.instruction: Notice that the canvas has no back: Frankenthaler poured paint so thin it sank into the raw fabric instead of sitting on the surface, staining the cloth like a giant watercolor. She was 23 when she made it, and the title tells you what to find — a landscape of mountains and sea dissolving into veils of blue and green.

name: Untitled (Stack) (1967)
teaser: Ten identical galvanized iron boxes, each exactly 9 inches tall, mounted one above another on the wall with 9-inch gaps — pure repetition, pure module. Judd called his works 'specific objects': neither painting nor sculpture, just things that exist in real space. The stack is Minimalism's logo: the same shape repeated until the wall becomes the sculpture.

exploreAction.targetName: Untitled (Stack) (1967) — the iron boxes on the wall
exploreAction.instruction: Count the rhythm: ten identical iron boxes march up the wall, each the same size, each separated by exactly the same gap — the repetition is the sculpture. Judd rejected both painting and sculpture and called these 'specific objects': real things in real space, made of industrial materials with no message and no metaphor. The stack turns the whole wall into the artwork, and your body measuring the height is part of it.

name: Double Negative (1969)
teaser: Two enormous cuts — 1,500 feet long and 50 feet deep — gouged into a mesa in the Nevada desert, moving 240,000 tons of rock. The artwork is not what was built but what was removed: two negative spaces facing each other across a gap. Owned by MoMA and sitting in the middle of nowhere, Double Negative is land art's most literal monument to absence.

exploreAction.targetName: Double Negative (1969) — the canyon made by removal
exploreAction.instruction: Walk the line of the cut: two trenches, each 1,500 feet long and 50 feet deep, carved into opposite sides of a mesa so they face each other across a gap — the sculpture is the space where the rock used to be. Heizer moved 240,000 tons of desert stone in 1969 and left the hole as the artwork.

name: Roden Crater (1979-)
teaser: James Turrell has spent more than forty years turning an extinct volcano in the Arizona desert into a naked-eye observatory — rooms, tunnels, and apertures engineered so the sky itself becomes the artwork: the sun, moon, and stars framed and manipulated through openings carved into the crater. Still incomplete, open only by reservation, it is the largest artwork ever made with light alone.

exploreAction.targetName: Roden Crater (1979-) — the volcano that holds the sky
exploreAction.instruction: Understand the trick of the rooms: Turrell has been carving this extinct volcano since 1979 into a series of chambers where the ceiling is a hole and the sky becomes a flat, colored disc — light that looks like a painting but is just atmosphere seen through engineered openings. One room is a perfect bowl that captures the dawn; another frames the moon at a precise angle.

name: Narcissus Garden (1966)
teaser: Kusama's first outdoor installation: 1,500 mirrored steel balls spread across the lawn of the Venice Biennale — and she sold them for two dollars each, a protest against the art market, until the Biennale stopped her. The mirrored orbs reflect the sky, the pavilions, and the viewer, a thousand small Narcissuses in the garden of art.

exploreAction.targetName: Narcissus Garden (1966) — the field of mirrors
exploreAction.instruction: Walk into the field of mirrors: 1,500 stainless steel balls stretch across the lawn, each one reflecting the sky, the pavilions, and you — a thousand small versions of Narcissus staring at themselves. Kusama made it for the 1966 Venice Biennale and immediately started selling the balls for two dollars each, a protest against an art world that priced everything and owned nothing. The Biennale shut her down, which was part of the performance.

name: Another Place (1997)
teaser: One hundred cast-iron figures — every one cast from Gormley's own body — stand on Crosby Beach near Liverpool, facing the horizon, staring out to sea. The tide covers them twice a day and they emerge again, barnacled, patient, anonymous. Each figure weighs about 650 kilograms, and the whole work is a meditation on time, mortality, and the shore between.

exploreAction.targetName: Another Place (1997) — the hundred iron men at sea
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the sea take them: a hundred iron men, all cast from Gormley's own body, stand in the surf at Crosby Beach facing the horizon. At low tide they stand chest-deep in sand; at high tide the water swallows them completely, and they re-emerge twice a day, covered in barnacles. Walk out to the farthest one and stand beside it — the figures are your height, your weight, your silence.

name: Comedian (2019)
teaser: A banana duct-taped to a wall with grey tape — sold at Art Basel Miami in 2019 for $120,000 (two editions plus a third at $150,000), and then eaten by a performance artist mid-display. Cattelan, the prankster of contemporary art, said: 'The banana is a banana.' It was the most argued-about artwork of the decade: is it a joke, a critique, or both?

exploreAction.targetName: Comedian (2019) — the banana and the tape
exploreAction.instruction: Decide what you are looking at: a single banana, duct-taped to a white wall with one strip of grey tape. Cattelan, who also made the golden toilet, said 'the banana is a banana.' Three editions sold for $120,000 to $150,000 at Art Basel Miami in 2019, and a performance artist walked up and ate the banana — the gallery replaced it.

name: The Garden of Earthly Delights (1500)
teaser: Hieronymus Bosch's triptych begins in Eden, swells into a surreal paradise crowded with naked figures and giant fruit, and ends in a black hell of instruments and torments. Nobody agrees on what it means.

exploreAction.targetName: The Garden of Earthly Delights (1500) by Bosch, center panel
exploreAction.instruction: Work left to right and resist reading it as a simple warning. Notice the oversized fruit, the glass domes, and the animals acting like people. Every object rewards a second look — the panel is a library of symbols with no index.

name: The Birth of Venus (1486)
teaser: Botticelli's Venus arrives on a shell, blown by wind gods and greeted by a handmaiden with a cloak. It was the first large-scale Renaissance painting of a nude Venus — pagan beauty made respectable by allegory.

exploreAction.targetName: The Birth of Venus (1486) by Botticelli, Uffizi
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Venus's pose — her weight on one leg, hands covering, hair long enough to reach the ground. Her body is idealized, elongated, and impossible: her neck and arms stretch beyond anatomy. That's the point — she is not a woman, she is an idea of beauty.

name: Dogs Playing Poker (1903)
teaser: Cassius Marcellus Coolidge's series of dogs around a card table became the most famous 'bad art' in America — and secretly a technical triumph of painting nine distinct canine personalities in one scene.

exploreAction.targetName: Dogs Playing Poker (1903) by Coolidge — 'A Friend in Need'
exploreAction.instruction: Look at each dog's face — the one slipping a card under the table, the one smoking a cigar, the one glaring. The jokes work because every dog has a distinct 'tell'. This is the most recognizable poker painting in history for a reason.

name: The Peacock Skirt (1893)
teaser: Aubrey Beardsley's sinuous black-and-white drawing of Salome in a peacock-patterned gown — an illustration for Oscar Wilde's play that scandalized Victorian England with its erotic decadence.

exploreAction.targetName: The Peacock Skirt (1893) by Beardsley
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how much is suggested with so little — the dress's eye-feathers, the figure's elongated neck, the halo-like headdress. Beardsley worked in pure black and white, and every empty space is as deliberate as every line.

name: Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1 (1871)
teaser: Whistler's portrait of his mother — he called it an 'arrangement', an experiment in color, not a portrait of a person. The Royal Academy hung it as 'Whistler's Mother', a title he hated, and it became one of the most parodied images in art.

exploreAction.targetName: Arrangement in Grey and Black (1871) by Whistler, Musée d'Orsay
exploreAction.instruction: Notice the composition: the mother is a flat silhouette against a patterned wall, her profile facing left, one foot on a stool. The frame is part of the artwork — Whistler designed it. Her hands, folded, hold a white handkerchief that is the brightest thing in the painting.

name: No. 5, 1948 (1948)
teaser: Jackson Pollock's most famous drip painting — eight feet of tangled black, gray, and brown skeins, the most expensive painting ever sold at the time ($140 million in 2006). Pollock painted it on the floor, from all sides, at the peak of his 'drip period'.

exploreAction.targetName: No. 5, 1948 (1948) by Pollock
exploreAction.instruction: Don't look for a subject — look for rhythm. Follow one black line through the tangle; it loops, crosses, returns. The painting has a center of gravity near the top, where the paint is thickest. Pollock said he was 'in' the painting while he worked: it is a record of movement, not a picture.

name: Red, Blue, Yellow (1929)
teaser: Mondrian's perfect grid: a red square dominating, two smaller yellow and blue squares, black lines of different thicknesses. The whole history of De Stijl in one image — art reduced to primary colors and straight lines.

exploreAction.targetName: Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow (1929) by Mondrian
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the black lines: they are not all the same thickness, and the grid does not continue past the canvas edge — the painting is a fragment of an infinite grid. The red block dominates by size, the yellow and blue balance it by placement. Mondrian removed everything else from art, and found peace.

name: The Bathers at Asnières (1884)
teaser: Seurat's young men lounging on the Seine shore at noon — painted with tiny dots of color that merge in the eye. It is the first great pointillist painting, made before Seurat finished inventing the method.

exploreAction.targetName: Bathers at Asnières (1884) by Seurat, National Gallery
exploreAction.instruction: Step close: the painting is dots — thousands of small marks. Step back: the dots fuse into solid figures. The boy in the water, the man with a pipe, the factories across the river — everyone is frozen in a Sunday stillness, painted with the science of color.

name: The Blue Rider (1903)
teaser: Kandinsky's early painting of a rider on a horse — the motif that gave the Blue Rider movement its name. Within a few years Kandinsky would dissolve the rider into pure color and become the father of abstraction.

exploreAction.targetName: The Blue Rider (1903) by Kandinsky
exploreAction.instruction: The rider is still recognizable, but look at how the horse is built from streaks of blue — the landscape is already breaking into color fields. Compare it to Kandinsky's later 'Composition VII': the rider disappears, and only the feeling of galloping remains.

name: The Ancient of Days (1794)
teaser: William Blake's frontispiece of an aged god leaning from a fiery disk to measure the void with a compass. It was Blake's favorite image, and he refused to say it was God — only 'the Ancient of Days,' the architect of the material world.

exploreAction.targetName: The Ancient of Days (1794) by Blake
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the compass: it measures the dark void below. The figure is bent, cramped, almost trapped inside the golden disk — Blake believed reason had imprisoned the imagination. The image is small, barely 23cm high, but its energy fills the whole page.

name: The Umbrellas (1886)
teaser: Renoir's Paris street crowded with umbrellas — half painted in his usual feathery style, half re-painted with crisp, linear strokes after a trip to Italy. The two halves are visibly different, and that difference is the whole painting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Umbrellas (1886) by Renoir, National Gallery
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the woman on the left holding a basket: she is painted with soft, blurry Impressionist strokes. The woman in the center is painted with firm outlines — Renoir repainted her years later. The painting is a conversation between two moments in his career.

name: The Peasant Wedding (1568)
teaser: Bruegel's chaotic feast in a barn — food being carried in on a door, musicians, a bride under a paper crown. Everyone is eating, and the painter is eating with his eyes: no one here is posed or idealized.

exploreAction.targetName: The Peasant Wedding (1568) by Bruegel, Kunsthistorisches Museum
exploreAction.instruction: Find the bride: she sits alone under the crown, hands folded, a small halo-like cloth behind her head — the only still figure in the room. Notice the porridge being carried on a door, the piper, the child licking a plate. Nobody is painted as noble or beautiful; they are simply alive.

name: The Ballet Class (1874)
teaser: Degas's rehearsal room full of young dancers in white tutus, a teacher with a stick, mothers knitting in the corner. The diagonal floor and the cropped edges make it feel like a photograph taken mid-moment — which it nearly is.

exploreAction.targetName: The Ballet Class (1874) by Degas, Musée d'Orsay
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the cutting: the dancer at the left edge is sliced in half, the stairs cut off — composition borrowed from Japanese prints and photography. The teacher is Jules Perrot, a famous ballet master. Degas painted dancers all his life; he said he saw them as 'human animals cleaning themselves.'

name: Untitled (1982) — the skull paintings
teaser: Jean-Michel Basquiat's crown-wearing skull in black, red, and yellow against a blue field — painted when he was 21. The crown is his signature: the artist as a self-made king of downtown New York.

exploreAction.targetName: Untitled (1982) skull painting by Basquiat
exploreAction.instruction: The skull's teeth are scattered, the eyes are red dashes, the crown floats above the head. Look at the texture: pencil lines, drips, patches of color left raw. Basquiat painted fast, layering graffiti energy over a deep knowledge of art history — the crown is a Van Gogh echo, an African motif, and a brand.

name: The Apparition (1876)
teaser: Gustave Moreau's Salome recoils as the severed head of John the Baptist appears, haloed, in a column of light — the most decadent religious painting of the century, dripping with jewels and shadow.

exploreAction.targetName: The Apparition (1876) by Moreau, Musée d'Orsay
exploreAction.instruction: The architecture is Mughal India, the jewels are oriental fantasy, the head floats in its own light. Salome points at it with one finger, her other hand frozen. Moreau painted desire and death as the same substance — the Symbolists worshipped him for it.

name: Echo and Narcissus (1903)
teaser: John William Waterhouse's Echo fades into the rocks — literally — while Narcissus kneels at his own reflection, already wasting away. It is Ovid's myth painted with pre-Raphaelite sensuality.

exploreAction.targetName: Echo and Narcissus (1903) by Waterhouse, Walker Art Gallery
exploreAction.instruction: Echo is dissolving into the cliff on the left — her feet, her arms, her torso becoming stone. Narcissus, kneeling on the right, is whole and beautiful. The stream runs between them: one is losing herself in him, he is losing himself in the water.

name: Self-Portrait at Twenty-Eight (1500)
teaser: Dürer painted himself dead-on, symmetrical, hand raised in blessing — the artist as Christ. It was the first autonomous self-portrait in Western art, and the first time an artist claimed his own image with divine authority.

exploreAction.targetName: Self-Portrait at Twenty-Eight (1500) by Dürer, Alte Pinakothek
exploreAction.instruction: The pose copies images of Christ — frontal, symmetrical, hand in blessing — and the fur collar turns his shoulders into a cloak. Dürer's hair falls like a Renaissance Christ's. He signed it with a monogram and the date, and wrote: 'I, Albrecht Dürer, painted myself.'

name: The Return of the Prodigal Son (1669)
teaser: Rembrandt's last great painting: the father, blind, embraces his ragged son while witnesses look on in shadow. Painted in his final year, it is a painting of forgiveness that took a lifetime to learn.

exploreAction.targetName: The Return of the Prodigal Son (1669) by Rembrandt, Hermitage
exploreAction.instruction: The father's hands are different: one is a man's hand, firm and strong; the other is softer, a mother's hand. His face is lit from within, old and blind with seeing. The son's shoes are worn through — he walked home barefoot. The witnesses in the shadows are painted loosely, almost unfinished; only the embrace is fully there.

name: Untitled (Black Square) (1915)
teaser: Malevich's black square on a white ground — painted after a lifetime of painting everything else. He called it 'the zero of form': the point where painting stops representing the world and becomes only itself. It hung in the corner of his exhibition like an icon.

exploreAction.targetName: Black Square (1915) by Malevich, Tretyakov Gallery
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the surface, not the shape: the black is not flat — brushstrokes, cracks, and a faint texture survive. Malevich hung it high in the corner of the room, the place Russians hang icons, facing the viewer like an altar. It is the end of painting and the beginning of everything after.

name: The Cardsharps (1595)
teaser: Caravaggio's teenage masterpiece: three men at a card table, and the boy on the right is cheating — he has an extra card behind his back and is signaling his accomplice. It is the first Caravaggio, painted when he was 24, and it already has his signature trick: light that reveals a secret.

exploreAction.targetName: The Cardsharps (1595) by Caravaggio, Kimbell Art Museum
exploreAction.instruction: The light falls on the young man's face first, then on the cheat's signal. The older cheat wears a glove with a slit — for sliding cards. Caravaggio froze the exact second of the con; the whole painting is a suspense story in one frame. Notice how the shadows are almost black — his signature tenebrism.

name: The Desperate Man (1845)
teaser: Gustave Courbet's self-portrait, eyes wild, hands tearing at his hair — painted when he was 26 and already broke. It is the most theatrical self-portrait of the century: the artist as a man barely containing his own energy.

exploreAction.targetName: The Desperate Man (1845) by Courbet
exploreAction.instruction: His fingers are buried in his hair, his eyes are wide open, and the canvas is lit from below like a stage. Courbet, the founder of Realism, painted himself at the extreme edge of feeling. He kept this painting with him all his life — it was his own favorite image of himself.

name: White Crucifixion (1938)
teaser: Marc Chagall's crucifixion with Jesus in a white prayer shawl, surrounded by fleeing refugees, a burning synagogue, and scenes of pogrom. Painted in 1938, it is one of the first artworks to read the Holocaust in advance.

exploreAction.targetName: White Crucifixion (1938) by Chagall, Art Institute of Chicago
exploreAction.instruction: Jesus is wrapped in a tallit — the Jewish prayer shawl — and his mother Mary stands beside him in a refugee's coat. Around the cross: a village on fire, a Torah scroll being carried, an old man fleeing with a sack. Chagall painted Jewish suffering as the crucifixion itself.

name: The Peaceable Kingdom (1834)
teaser: Edward Hicks painted the lion lying down with the lamb over 60 times — the same composition, the same message of peace, repainted for his entire life. He was a Quaker preacher who painted between sermons.

exploreAction.targetName: The Peaceable Kingdom (1834) by Hicks
exploreAction.instruction: The foreground shows Isaiah's prophecy — wolf and lamb, leopard and kid, a child leading them. The background shows William Penn signing a treaty with the Lenape, the Quakers' hope made visible. Hicks was a self-taught folk painter; his flat, glowing animals are as sincere as art gets.

name: Christina's World (1948) — the original
teaser: Andrew Wyeth's painting of a woman lying in a field, looking toward a farmhouse on a hill — based on his neighbor Anna Christina Olson, who crawled everywhere because polio had paralyzed her legs. The painting hides the story; the pose tells it.

exploreAction.targetName: Christina's World (1948) by Wyeth, MoMA
exploreAction.instruction: The house is far; the grass is huge. Christina is not resting — she is dragging herself toward the house, her thin arms and sunken back the only clues. Wyeth painted the field's dry grass blade by blade. He called the painting a portrait of courage, and he never showed her face.

name: Mont Sainte-Victoire (1904)
teaser: Cézanne painted the same mountain from the same window over 60 times — each version a new attempt to hold the mountain's mass in paint. In the late versions, the mountain dissolves into facets that would become Cubism.

exploreAction.targetName: Mont Sainte-Victoire (1904) by Cézanne, Philadelphia Museum
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how the mountain is built from small flat planes of color — greens, ochres, blues — that lock together like masonry. Cézanne said he wanted to 'make of Impressionism something solid and durable, like the art of the museums.' Picasso called him 'the father of us all.'

name: The Migration of the Negro (1941)
teaser: Jacob Lawrence's series of 60 small panels telling the story of the Great Migration — six million Black Americans leaving the South for northern cities between 1910 and 1940. Each panel is a chapter; the series is an epic in tempera.

exploreAction.targetName: The Migration Series (1941) by Lawrence — panels 1-6
exploreAction.instruction: Panel 1: the massed figures wait at the station. Panel 3: the lynched figure against a red sky. Lawrence used flat, angular shapes and the same colors throughout so the series reads as one long pulse. He was 23 when he painted it, in a Harlem studio, in three months.

name: The Embrace (1903)
teaser: Gustav Klimt's golden couple, entangled — their bodies dissolve into ornament, faces real. It is Klimt's celebration of love as the one thing that stays human in a world of pattern.

exploreAction.targetName: The Embrace (1903) by Klimt
exploreAction.instruction: The two figures are one shape: his robe and hers flow together into a single golden mass. Only their faces and hands are painted realistically. Klimt used real gold leaf — the patterns sparkle differently as you move. The pattern on her dress is the same eye-motif from The Kiss.

name: The Avenue at Middelharnis (1689)
teaser: Hobberna's straight avenue of poplars vanishing toward a village — the most famous one-point perspective in landscape painting, admired by Constable and copied for two centuries.

exploreAction.targetName: The Avenue at Middelharnis (1689) by Hobbema, National Gallery
exploreAction.instruction: Walk the road with your eyes: the trees line up exactly, the sky opens at the vanishing point. The painting is a hymn to order and to the quiet life of a Dutch village — the dirt road, the pollarded trees, the tiny figures with a dog.

name: The Rokeby Venus (1647)
teaser: Velázquez's only surviving nude — Venus reclining, seen from behind, her face reflected in a mirror held by Cupid. The blurred reflection is the painting's magic: we see her face without ever turning her toward us.

exploreAction.targetName: The Rokeby Venus (1647) by Velázquez, National Gallery
exploreAction.instruction: Her face in the mirror is soft, unfocused — Velázquez painted the reflection as a memory, not a portrait. The sheets are silver-gray, her skin the only warm color. In 1914 a suffragette slashed it with a meat cleaver; the cuts were repaired so well they are nearly invisible.

name: Judith Beheading Holofernes (1599)
teaser: Caravaggio's Judith grimaces as she saws through the general's neck while her maid waits with a sack — blood sprays, the bed sheets darken. It is the most violent painting of a Bible story ever made until that point.

exploreAction.targetName: Judith Beheading Holofernes (1599) by Caravaggio, Palazzo Barberini
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the three faces: Judith's wrinkled nose and open mouth — the physical effort of the act — the maid's calm readiness, and Holofernes' twisted shout. The blood arcs in a line Caravaggio studied from real anatomy. He painted violence as news, not allegory.

name: The Entombment of Christ (1604)
teaser: Caravaggio's mourners lower Christ's body toward the viewer — the stone slab at the bottom edge points straight at us, making us the tomb. It is a painting that pulls the sacred into the present.

exploreAction.targetName: The Entombment of Christ (1604) by Caravaggio, Vatican
exploreAction.instruction: The slab juts out of the picture toward your feet — Caravaggio makes the viewer part of the scene. The figures are lit like a stage, the body heavy in the arms of the men who carry it. Mary's hands are raised in grief; her gesture is the painting's silent scream.

name: Bacchus (1596)
teaser: Caravaggio's young god of wine lounges with a glass of wine and a bowl of fruit — but the fruit is rotting, the wine is murky, and Bacchus himself looks tired. Caravaggio's gods are always a little sick.

exploreAction.targetName: Bacchus (1596) by Caravaggio, Uffizi
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the still life first: the pomegranate is split, the grapes are browning, a fig is burst — decay mid-picture. Bacchus holds the glass with dirty fingernails. Caravaggio painted pleasure with its expiration date visible.

name: The Fortune Teller (1594)
teaser: A young man offers his palm to a Romani fortune teller while she quietly slips the ring off his finger. Caravaggio's first genre scene — a pickpocket joke painted with the dignity of an altarpiece.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fortune Teller (1594) by Caravaggio, Louvre
exploreAction.instruction: Follow the hands: his glove is half off, her fingers work the ring. The two figures face each other like a duel — honesty and theft meeting palm to palm. Caravaggio painted this when he was poor, and it made his name.

name: Narcissus (1599)
teaser: Caravaggio's Narcissus kneels at a dark pool, his reflection touching his own hand — the circle of self-love closed into a perfect ring. It is one of only two known Caravaggios on a myth subject.

exploreAction.targetName: Narcissus (1599) by Caravaggio, Palazzo Barberini
exploreAction.instruction: His elbows frame the pool, and his reflection is exactly symmetrical — the two figures almost form a complete circle. The water is black, the light is cold. Caravaggio paints the moment of falling in love with yourself, and it already looks like drowning.

name: Saint Jerome Writing (1606)
teaser: Caravaggio's saint, an old man with a skull and a candle, writes in a shaft of light — the skull and the quill, death and translation, sharing the desk. It is a painting about work done in the face of death.

exploreAction.targetName: Saint Jerome Writing (1606) by Caravaggio, Galleria Borghese
exploreAction.instruction: The light comes from a source we cannot see, falling only on the book, the hands, and the forehead. The skull sits at the corner like a colleague. Jerome translated the Bible; Caravaggio paints the desk where eternity gets written down.

name: Boy with a Basket of Fruit (1593)
teaser: Caravaggio's teenage boy offers a basket of fruit so fresh the leaves are still veined — a perfect still life on top of a perfect portrait. It may be the painter himself, at the start of his career.

exploreAction.targetName: Boy with a Basket of Fruit (1593) by Caravaggio, Galleria Borghese
exploreAction.instruction: The fruit is so carefully painted it has its own light — grapes, apples, figs, a pomegranate, each leaf with its veins. The boy's face is soft, almost feminine, his shoulder bare. The basket's shadow on the wall is painted as carefully as the boy.

name: Saint Francis in Meditation (1606)
teaser: Caravaggio's monk holds a skull in the dark — no halo, no miracle, just a man contemplating what the skull means. It is the most purely human of all his religious paintings.

exploreAction.targetName: Saint Francis in Meditation (1606) by Caravaggio
exploreAction.instruction: The skull faces the viewer, not Francis — we are the ones being asked. His hands rest on the bone like a man steadying himself. The robe and the darkness swallow the background; the face, the hands, and the skull are all that remain.

name: Amor Victorious (1602)
teaser: Caravaggio's naked Cupid grins while trampling the symbols of human achievement — musical instruments, books, armor, a laurel crown. Love defeats everything, and the boy knows it.

exploreAction.targetName: Amor Victorious (1602) by Caravaggio, Gemäldegalerie Berlin
exploreAction.instruction: The boy's grin is knowing, almost cruel — he has already won. Under his foot: a violin, a compass, a book, armor, a crown. His wings are a real eagle's, painted from a specimen. Caravaggio painted love as a punk with a quiver.

name: The Incredulity of Saint Thomas (1602)
teaser: Caravaggio's doubting Thomas puts his finger into Christ's side wound while the other apostles crowd to look — the moment belief becomes empirical. It scandalized some and thrilled everyone else.

exploreAction.targetName: The Incredulity of Saint Thomas (1602) by Caravaggio, Sanssouci
exploreAction.instruction: Christ guides Thomas's hand into the wound — the touch is the whole subject. The four heads press together like a medical consultation. Caravaggio painted doubt as the honest path: Thomas must check, and Christ lets him.

name: The Seven Works of Mercy (1607)
teaser: Caravaggio's single canvas shows all seven acts of mercy happening at once — a naked man, a corpse carried feet-first, a woman breastfeeding her father in prison, a pilgrim drinking. The city of Naples is the stage.

exploreAction.targetName: The Seven Works of Mercy (1607) by Caravaggio, Pio Monte della Misericordia
exploreAction.instruction: Try to find all seven acts: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, sheltering the stranger, visiting the sick, visiting the imprisoned, burying the dead. The winged angel in the center pushes two men down — mercy is heavy work.

name: Saint John the Baptist (1602)
teaser: Caravaggio's teenage Baptist lounges in a dark landscape with a ram — half saint, half shepherd boy, wholly sensual. The church complained; Caravaggio painted sainthood with a body, not just a halo.

exploreAction.targetName: Saint John the Baptist (1602) by Caravaggio, Capitoline Museums
exploreAction.instruction: The boy smiles at something only he can see. The ram, the staff, the animal-skin wrap: the symbols of the Baptist. Caravaggio's saints are street kids in studio light — that was the scandal, and it is the power.

name: The Burial of Saint Lucy (1608)
teaser: Caravaggio's last years in Sicily: two gravediggers lower the saint's body into the earth while mourners stand at the top of a staircase — grief from below, seen as if we are in the grave.

exploreAction.targetName: The Burial of Saint Lucy (1608) by Caravaggio, Syracuse
exploreAction.instruction: We see the burial from inside the pit — the mourners are silhouettes at the top, the gravediggers bend over the saint. The composition is brutal and bare, painted during Caravaggio's flight as a fugitive. He made death look like the literal ground beneath everyone.

name: The Adoration of the Shepherds (1609)
teaser: Caravaggio's last nativity: shepherds crowd around the newborn in a bare room, Mary exhausted, Joseph a working man. No gold, no glory — just birth in a shed, painted by a man on the run.

exploreAction.targetName: The Adoration of the Shepherds (1609) by Caravaggio, Messina
exploreAction.instruction: The light comes from the baby himself — the only bright thing in the dark shed. The shepherds' faces are rough, their hands are working hands. Caravaggio stripped the nativity of every decoration; what remains is a family and some animals and a light.

name: The Denial of Saint Peter (1610)
teaser: Caravaggio's Peter, three-fingered hand raised in denial, leans into a circle of lamplight while a soldier and a woman watch. It is among his very last paintings, and it shows a man who has failed the test.

exploreAction.targetName: The Denial of Saint Peter (1610) by Caravaggio, Metropolitan Museum
exploreAction.instruction: The three fingers up — the third denial, exactly as Peter warned. His face is lit from below by the fire, guilty already. The two others lean in, pressing the question. Caravaggio painted this while dying, alone, in 1610.

name: David with the Head of Goliath (1610)
teaser: Caravaggio's David holds Goliath's severed head at arm's length — and the head is Caravaggio's own face, painted during his last year as a condemned fugitive. The victim is the artist.

exploreAction.targetName: David with the Head of Goliath (1610) by Caravaggio, Galleria Borghese
exploreAction.instruction: Look closely at the head: it is Caravaggio's self-portrait, eyes open, mouth slack — the fugitive painting his own death warrant. David's face is sad, not triumphant. He sent the painting to the Pope as a plea for pardon. The pardon arrived days after Caravaggio died.

name: The Martyrdom of Saint Ursula (1610)
teaser: Caravaggio's final painting: the moment an arrow pierces Ursula's chest while the king watches — the saint's face in shock, the arrow already through. He painted it in Naples, weeks before his death.

exploreAction.targetName: The Martyrdom of Saint Ursula (1610) by Caravaggio, Naples
exploreAction.instruction: The arrow has just entered — her lips part, her hand rises in a frozen gesture. The archer-king looks on with something like regret. Painted in Caravaggio's final weeks, it is a self-portrait of dying: the moment the world's arrow arrives.

name: Young Sick Bacchus (1593)
teaser: Caravaggio's early self-portrait as a green-skinned Bacchus — a feverish young man in a sheet, offering grapes with an unwell smile. He painted himself as the god of wine while recovering from illness.

exploreAction.targetName: Young Sick Bacchus (1593) by Caravaggio, Galleria Borghese
exploreAction.instruction: The skin is sallow, the gaze is glazed — this is sickness, not ecstasy. The grapes he offers are overripe. Caravaggio painted his own face as the god of wine, and the joke is on the gods: even Bacchus gets the flu.

name: Rest on the Flight into Egypt (1597)
teaser: Caravaggio's holy family pauses on the run — Joseph holds the score for a singing angel while Mary and the child sleep against a donkey. Music, exhaustion, and escape in one quiet moment.

exploreAction.targetName: Rest on the Flight into Egypt (1597) by Caravaggio, Galleria Doria Pamphilj
exploreAction.instruction: The angel plays a violin from behind — the music is the painting's light source. Joseph holds the open score; Mary sleeps wrapped in red. It is one of Caravaggio's gentlest works, painted before he turned to blood.

name: The Crowning with Thorns (1602)
teaser: Caravaggio's soldiers press a thorn crown onto Christ's head with canes, four hands working like a machine. The cruelty is bureaucratic — they are just doing their job.

exploreAction.targetName: The Crowning with Thorns (1602) by Caravaggio, Kunsthistorisches Museum
exploreAction.instruction: Two soldiers hold the canes, pushing the crown down — the third leans in to inspect. Christ's eyes are closed, his hands tied. The faces of the soldiers are ordinary, focused, almost bored. That is the point: cruelty needs no monsters.

name: The Taking of Christ (1602)
teaser: Caravaggio's arrest scene — Judas kisses Christ while soldiers close in, and a man at the edge raises a lantern and his arms, witnessing everything. The light reveals the betrayal like a flashbulb.

exploreAction.targetName: The Taking of Christ (1602) by Caravaggio, National Gallery of Ireland
exploreAction.instruction: The man with the lantern at the far right is a self-portrait — Caravaggio as the witness who sees but does nothing. Christ's hands are folded in calm; Judas's kiss lands on his cheek. The armor of the soldier glints with the lantern light: the whole scene is lit by the betrayal.

name: The Flagellation of Christ (1607)
teaser: Caravaggio's Christ is tied to a column while three men take turns with the whip — the faces of the tormentors hidden or turned away, the body the only clear thing in the dark.

exploreAction.targetName: The Flagellation of Christ (1607) by Caravaggio, Naples
exploreAction.instruction: The light falls on Christ's back, already striped. The torturers' faces are cut off by the frame or turned aside — they are not individuals, they are the machinery of punishment. Painted in Naples, it is one of Caravaggio's most brutal and most silent works.

name: The Martyrdom of Saint Matthew (1600)
teaser: Caravaggio's altar for the Contarelli Chapel: an assassin lunges at the fallen Matthew while a naked youth flees and onlookers scatter — violence staged in a church, painted with a street brawler's energy.

exploreAction.targetName: The Martyrdom of Saint Matthew (1600) by Caravaggio, San Luigi dei Francesi
exploreAction.instruction: The killer holds Matthew down, his sword ready; Matthew reaches up, accepting. The crowd recoils in a wave. The boy at the left — a self-portrait — runs from the scene. Caravaggio's martyrs die in the middle of the street, not in heaven.

name: The Conversion of Saint Paul (1601)
teaser: Caravaggio's Paul lies flat under a rearing horse, blinded by a light from off-canvas — the road to Damascus reduced to a man, a horse, and a beam of light. The horse takes up most of the painting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Conversion of Saint Paul (1601) by Caravaggio, Santa Maria del Popolo
exploreAction.instruction: The horse is the largest thing in the frame; Paul is crushed beneath, arms out, a man who has been knocked flat by the truth. The light comes from nowhere visible — it simply happens. No road, no Damascus, no witnesses: just the moment.

name: The Crucifixion of Saint Peter (1601)
teaser: Caravaggio's Peter is nailed upside down while three workers strain to raise the cross — the saint's face turned to us, the labor of execution laid bare. Crucifixion as a heavy, sweaty job.

exploreAction.targetName: The Crucifixion of Saint Peter (1601) by Caravaggio, Santa Maria del Popolo
exploreAction.instruction: The three men haul the cross up with their whole bodies — this is manual labor, filmed in a cellar. Peter's eyes meet ours. He asked to be crucified upside down, unworthy of Christ's death. Caravaggio paints the humility as physical fact.

name: The Deposition (1604)
teaser: Caravaggio's Pietà without Mary — three men lower Christ's body while a woman behind them howls with her arms up. The composition is a slow, painful ladder of grief from top to bottom.

exploreAction.targetName: The Deposition (1604) by Caravaggio, Vatican
exploreAction.instruction: Follow the arms: each figure holds Christ at a different height, forming a diagonal of grief. The woman behind — the weeping Mary — throws her arms wide and back, the painting's rawest gesture. The stone slab at the bottom points out at the viewer: the body is coming toward you.

name: The Annunciation (1608)
teaser: Caravaggio's angel swoops in from the left, wings still beating, finger pointed — while Mary receives the news with a hand raised in a gesture that could be acceptance or protest. It is an annunciation with tension.

exploreAction.targetName: The Annunciation (1608) by Caravaggio, Musée des Beaux-Arts de Nancy
exploreAction.instruction: The angel is mid-flight, robe streaming, arriving like a report. Mary's raised hand is ambiguous — a greeting, a question, a shield. Painted during Caravaggio's flight from Rome, it is an annunciation to a man in hiding: news always arrives.

name: The Penitent Magdalene (1597)
teaser: Caravaggio's Magdalene sits on the floor with a jar of ointment and her jewelry abandoned beside her — a teenage woman, exhausted, who has just made a decision. The tear on her cheek is the painting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Penitent Magdalene (1597) by Caravaggio, Galleria Doria Pamphilj
exploreAction.instruction: Her eyes are swollen, her head bowed — she has been crying for a long time. The pearls and the jar are at her feet, already given up. Caravaggio painted his friend, a courtesan, as the saint; the model's own story made the painting possible.

name: The Beheading of Saint John the Baptist (1608)
teaser: Caravaggio's largest painting and his only signed work — the signature is written in the blood pooling from John's neck. The executioner grips the head by the hair while Salome holds the basin.

exploreAction.targetName: The Beheading of Saint John the Baptist (1608) by Caravaggio, Valletta
exploreAction.instruction: Find the signature: 'f. Michelang.o' written in the red pool at the bottom — blood as ink. The executioner has his knee on John's back, the head hangs, the two onlookers at the window stare blankly. It was painted for the Knights of Malta while Caravaggio was their prisoner.

name: Judith and Holofernes (1612)
teaser: Gentileschi's Judith saws through Holofernes' neck with the maid pressing him down — painted by a woman who knew violence firsthand. It is the most visceral Judith in art history.

exploreAction.targetName: Judith and Holofernes (1612) by Gentileschi, Uffizi
exploreAction.instruction: Both women are in the fight — Judith pulls the sword, the maid shoves the general's head down onto the blade. The blood sprays across the sheets in an arc. Gentileschi painted this after her own trial; the painting is her testimony in oil.

name: The Burial at Ornans (1850)
teaser: Courbet's ten-foot canvas of a village funeral — the priest, the gravedigger, the mourners in black, and a dog, all painted life-size without any of the nobility painting usually demanded. Realism was declared a movement.

exploreAction.targetName: The Burial at Ornans (1850) by Courbet, Musée d'Orsay
exploreAction.instruction: Count the mourners and watch how their faces are ordinary, tired, individual. Courbet painted his own hometown funeral — the people are real, the grief is real, and no one is posed like a saint. The critics called it ugly. That was the point.

name: The Card Players (1893)
teaser: Cézanne's two Provençal peasants face each other over a card table — a bottle, two pipes, and the whole weight of concentration. He painted the series over five years, reducing life to its essentials.

exploreAction.targetName: The Card Players (1893) by Cézanne, Courtauld Gallery
exploreAction.instruction: There is no story — just two men, a table, and attention. Look at how the tabletop tilts toward you while the men stay vertical; Cézanne compressed space on purpose. The bottle is the third player, standing perfectly still in the center.

name: The Valley of the Shadow of Death (1855)
teaser: Roger Fenton's photograph of a Crimean War road littered with cannonballs — the first great war photograph. It shows what the battlefield looks like after everyone has gone home.

exploreAction.targetName: The Valley of the Shadow of Death (1855) by Fenton
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the road: it curves away, empty, its edges dense with round black cannonballs. Fenton hauled a wagon of glass plates to the Crimea and made this after the battle, when the valley was quiet. It is war photographed as aftermath — no hero, no enemy, only objects.

name: The Sleepers (1866)
teaser: Courbet's two women tangled in sleep on a bed — painted for a collector of erotica, and still the most openly sensual painting of two women in the nineteenth century. It was hidden from public view for decades.

exploreAction.targetName: The Sleepers (1866) by Courbet, Petit Palais
exploreAction.instruction: The two bodies make one shape — dark hair against red, the sheet draping like a wave. Courbet painted skin with the same weight he painted stone. The pearls on the table are a classical hint; the painting itself needed no hint at all.

name: The Horse Fair (1855)
teaser: Rosa Bonheur's enormous painting of horses surging from a Paris fair — she attended in men's clothes to sketch freely, a woman who had to fight for the right to paint at all.

exploreAction.targetName: The Horse Fair (1855) by Bonheur, Metropolitan Museum
exploreAction.instruction: The horses pour diagonally across the canvas — whites, blacks, bays — their riders leaning in. Bonheur studied anatomy at slaughterhouses to get the muscles right. It was her most famous work, toured across two continents, and made her rich.

name: The Gates of Hell (1917)
teaser: Rodin's unfinished masterpiece — a doorway crowded with 180 figures of love and torment, from The Thinker brooding at the top to Paolo and Francesca embracing below. He worked on it for 37 years and never finished.

exploreAction.targetName: The Gates of Hell (1917) by Rodin, Musée Rodin
exploreAction.instruction: Start at the top: The Thinker sits above the door — not a philosopher but Dante, or Rodin himself, watching the crowd below. Work your way down through the couples, the fallen, the reaching hands. Many of Rodin's most famous sculptures were pulled from this doorway as fragments.

name: Moose in the Gaspé (1937)
teaser: Clarence Gagnon's snowy moose in the Quebec woods — the painter who illustrated Louis Hémon's Maria Chapdelaine and made the Canadian landscape his lifelong subject.

exploreAction.targetName: Moose in the Gaspé (1937) by Gagnon
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the blue snow shadows and the moose standing in the clearing — Gagnon's colors are northern and precise. He painted the Quebec that was vanishing around him: the farms, the forests, the animals, the light.

name: The Persistence of Memory — the original (1931)
teaser: Dalí's melting watches over the Catalonian coast, painted in a few hours after watching Camembert soften in the sun. He refused to explain it; the watches were simply 'the softness of time.'

exploreAction.targetName: The Persistence of Memory (1931) by Dalí, MoMA — the original
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the creature with eyelashes in the center — Dalí's own face in profile, melting into the ground. The only hard object is the one watch that has not melted; it lies face-down, crawling with ants, the artist's symbol for decay. The landscape is the real coast of Catalonia.

name: Sleeping Venus (1510)
teaser: Giorgione's goddess sleeps in a landscape, her hand behind her head — the first large reclining nude in Western painting, and the model for every Venus that followed, from Titian to Manet.

exploreAction.targetName: Sleeping Venus (1510) by Giorgione, Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister
exploreAction.instruction: Her body makes a long diagonal against the hills — the landscape seems to continue her curves. Giorgione died at 32, possibly leaving this unfinished; the landscape may be by Titian. The painting invented a genre: the goddess asleep, watched by the viewer.

name: The Tempest (1508)
teaser: Giorgione's soldier and naked woman face each other across a stream while lightning forks behind them — nobody agrees on what is happening. It is the first painting that seems to exist purely for its own mystery.

exploreAction.targetName: The Tempest (1508) by Giorgione, Accademia Venice
exploreAction.instruction: The woman nurses a child; the soldier stands apart; the storm arrives. Is it Adam and Eve? A soldier and his wife? A myth? The painting resists every answer. X-rays show Giorgione painted a different woman here originally — he changed his own mystery.

name: The Lady with the Unicorn (1506)
teaser: Raphael's young woman holds a small unicorn, a symbol of chastity and a wedding gift — the unicorn's horn was later painted over and only restored in the twentieth century.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lady with the Unicorn (1506) by Raphael, Galleria Borghese
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the unicorn: small, white, resting in her arms. Raphael balanced it against the famous Mona Lisa — the pose, the loggia, the landscape echo Leonardo. The unicorn was added later, covering an earlier dog; the painting is a palimpsest of a wedding.

name: Danaë (1553)
teaser: Titian's Danaë receives the golden rain of Zeus — the first version painted for a cardinal, who was so shocked he had it exchanged for a picture of a dog.

exploreAction.targetName: Danaë (1553) by Titian, Prado
exploreAction.instruction: Danaë lies on white sheets, catching the golden coins with her body — Zeus as money, and the gods reduced to wealth. The old woman behind gathers the coins in her apron. Titian painted sensuality, commerce, and myth in one warm glow.

name: Bacchus and Ariadne (1523)
teaser: Titian's Bacchus leaps from his chariot toward Ariadne, abandoned on Naxos — he loves her at first sight, and the whole painting is that leap frozen mid-air.

exploreAction.targetName: Bacchus and Ariadne (1523) by Titian, National Gallery
exploreAction.instruction: Bacchus is mid-jump, his leopard-skin billowing, a cheetah at his feet; Ariadne's arm is raised in surprise. The sky is ultramarine — the pigment was more expensive than gold. Titian spent two years on the sky alone, and it shows.

name: The Death of Actaeon (1559)
teaser: Titian's hunter is torn apart by his own dogs after seeing Diana naked — the painting shows the moment the hounds turn on their master, the myth's cruelty made lush.

exploreAction.targetName: The Death of Actaeon (1559) by Titian, National Gallery
exploreAction.instruction: Actaeon falls backward, already part deer — antlers rising from his head — while his own dogs bite. Diana, in the distance, looses the fatal arrow. Titian painted the late 'poesie' series for King Philip II; these are myths painted as fate.

name: Self-Portrait at 63 (1669)
teaser: Rembrandt's last self-portrait — an old man with a paintbrush, looking at us with total calm. He painted about 80 self-portraits across his life; this is the final word, made in his year of death.

exploreAction.targetName: Self-Portrait at 63 (1669) by Rembrandt, National Gallery
exploreAction.instruction: The paint is applied in thick slabs and thin glazes — you can see the brush moving, the palette knife scraping. His hands hold the tools of the trade. The face is unsparing: the skin, the eyes, the history. It is not a portrait of an old man; it is a portrait of looking.

name: The Lion Hunt (1616)
teaser: Rubens' hunters attack a cornered lion with spears from horseback — the Baroque's most ferocious hunting scene, painted at the peak of his powers and his physical bulk.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lion Hunt (1616) by Rubens, Alte Pinakothek
exploreAction.instruction: The composition is a whirlwind: horse and lion spiral around each other, spears crossing, manes flying. Rubens kept live lions for study and borrowed them for the studio. The violence is choreographed — every muscle is a dancing line.

name: The Three Graces (1635)
teaser: Rubens' three goddesses in a golden ring, painted when he was nearly sixty and still painting flesh like a young man in love with it. His second wife modeled for the central figure.

exploreAction.targetName: The Three Graces (1635) by Rubens, Prado
exploreAction.instruction: The three women hold hands in a circle, their bodies painted in pearl-pink and gold. Rubens' women are famously substantial — he loved the weight of flesh. The central Grace is thought to be Hélène Fourment, his wife, who was 30 years younger than him.

name: The Lamentation of Christ (1604)
teaser: Caravaggio's mourners lift Christ's body toward us, Mary's arms spread in silent grief. The slab at the bottom juts into our space — the viewer is standing at the tomb.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lamentation (1604) by Caravaggio, Vatican Museums
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the figures form a diagonal from the reaching Mary down to the slab — the composition pushes the body toward the viewer. Mary's arms are raised like wings, John the Baptist steadies Christ's back. The light is theatrical, the grief is domestic.

name: The Flagellation of Christ — Piero della Francesca (1460)
teaser: Piero's tiny panel splits into two scenes: the flagellation in the foreground, three men talking in the background. Scholars have argued for centuries about who the three men are — it may be a political allegory of the fallen Byzantine Empire.

exploreAction.targetName: The Flagellation of Christ (1460) by Piero della Francesca, Urbino
exploreAction.instruction: The foreground column is lit by two different light sources — the scene is a mathematical puzzle of perspective, and the geometry is the message. The three men in the background may be a real political event of 1453. Piero painted like an architect who believed God was a geometer.

name: The Baptism of Christ (1450)
teaser: Piero della Francesca's Christ stands in the Jordan while John pours water and three angels watch — the dove descends, the landscape is pure geometry. Painting as theology and mathematics at once.

exploreAction.targetName: The Baptism of Christ (1450) by Piero della Francesca, National Gallery
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the symmetry: Christ is the exact center, the dove above him, John at his side, the three angels in a row like a musical chord. The light is even and eternal — no drama, only certainty. Piero painted the calm at the heart of belief.

name: The Entombment of Atala (1808)
teaser: Anne-Louis Girodet's Chateaubriand heroine is lowered into a cave tomb by a missionary and a lover — a Romantic novel painted as a pietà, grief arranged like a stage set.

exploreAction.targetName: The Entombment of Atala (1808) by Girodet, Louvre
exploreAction.instruction: Atala's body is lit from below like a candle — her white dress glows against the dark cave. The missionary supports her, the lover kisses her hand. Girodet turned a sentimental novel into a religious painting, and the formula made him rich.

name: The Death of Sardanapalus (1827)
teaser: Delacroix's Assyrian king watches from his bed as his treasures, horses, and concubines are destroyed on his orders — an orgy of destruction painted in burning red. Byron's play, painted as the end of the world.

exploreAction.targetName: The Death of Sardanapalus (1827) by Delacroix, Louvre
exploreAction.instruction: The king lies back, detached, while below him bodies fall, a horse rears, an elephant stampedes, and a slave stabs himself. Delacroix fills the frame edge to edge — no escape, no sky. It is the Romantic imagination at maximum temperature.

name: Wanderer in the Fog — Caspar David Friedrich variations (1818)
teaser: Friedrich's other fog paintings — a man facing a sea of cloud, a lone tree in a field — show the same Romantic creed: the self is small, nature is infinite, and the view is a feeling.

exploreAction.targetName: Friedrich's fog landscapes (1818) — the sea of clouds view
exploreAction.instruction: The man is seen from behind, so we see what he sees: a sea of fog with mountains rising like islands. Friedrich painted the back of a figure so the viewer could stand in their shoes. It is a painting about the experience of looking, not the view.

name: The Lonely Tree (1822)
teaser: Friedrich's single oak in a field at sunset, a shepherd and his flock passing beneath — a tree as a witness to centuries, painted as a portrait of time itself.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lonely Tree (1822) by Friedrich, Alte Nationalgalerie
exploreAction.instruction: The oak bends like an old man, stripped of leaves, its branches like veins against the orange sky. The tiny figures below make the tree enormous. Friedrich painted the tree's stubbornness — it has outlived storms, and it will outlive us.

name: Chalk Cliffs on Rügen (1818)
teaser: Friedrich's white cliffs, a man peering over the edge, a woman pointing at two tiny sailboats below. Painted on his honeymoon — and the edge of the cliff is the real subject.

exploreAction.targetName: Chalk Cliffs on Rügen (1818) by Friedrich, Kunst Museum Winterthur
exploreAction.instruction: One figure kneels at the edge, one leans, one points — three responses to the drop. The white chalk glows against the blue sea. Friedrich married the painter Caroline Bommer that year; the painting is a honeymoon photograph of the abyss.

name: Two Men Contemplating the Moon (1819)
teaser: Friedrich's two men on a rocky path, seen from behind, staring at a crescent moon through a dead tree. The same theme — humans small, sky vast — that he painted his whole life.

exploreAction.targetName: Two Men Contemplating the Moon (1819) by Friedrich
exploreAction.instruction: The two figures are often read as Friedrich and his friend. They lean together, sharing the view. The moon is a thin crescent; the tree is dead; the path leads nowhere. Friedrich painted companionship inside solitude.

name: The Monk by the Sea (1809)
teaser: Friedrich's tiny monk stands at the edge of a sea that fills three-quarters of the canvas — sky, water, sand, and one small figure. It is the most radical emptiness in painting before the twentieth century.

exploreAction.targetName: The Monk by the Sea (1809) by Friedrich, Alte Nationalgalerie
exploreAction.instruction: The monk is a speck — you may need to search for him. The sky and sea are almost the same tone, a wall of silence. Kleist said looking at it felt like having your eyelids cut off: you are alone with the infinite.

name: Landscape with the Fall of Icarus (1560)
