teaser: Bruegel's Icarus splashes into the sea in the corner while a farmer plows, a shepherd stares at the sky, and a ship sails on — nobody stops. It may not even be Bruegel, and it is the most famous depiction of indifference in art.

exploreAction.targetName: Landscape with the Fall of Icarus (1560) by Bruegel, Musées Royaux Brussels
exploreAction.instruction: Look for Icarus: just two white legs kicking in the water beside the ship. The plowman works on; the sun shines; the world does not stop for the boy who flew too high. The poem by W.H. Auden — 'About suffering they were never wrong, the Old Masters' — is about this exact painting.

name: The Massacre of the Innocents (1567)
teaser: Bruegel's soldiers enter a Flemish village to seize children from mothers — painted as a biblical scene but read as a Spanish atrocity in the Netherlands. The horror is in the everyday setting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Massacre of the Innocents (1567) by Bruegel, Kunsthistorisches Museum
exploreAction.instruction: The soldiers are not monsters — they are soldiers doing a job in a winter village. Mothers struggle, a horse rears, snow falls. Bruegel set a massacre in a place that looks like home, and that is what makes it unbearable.

name: The Blind Leading the Blind (1568)
teaser: Bruegel's line of six blind men follows their leader into a ditch — each already at a different stage of falling. It illustrates a Bible verse and the human condition at once.

exploreAction.targetName: The Blind Leading the Blind (1568) by Bruegel, Museo di Capodimonte
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the chain of falls: the first man is already down, the second is mid-fall, the third is stumbling, the last still walking upright. Bruegel painted each stage of disaster. The church steeple in the background is the destination they will never reach.

name: The Harvesters (1565)
teaser: Bruegel's wheat field at harvest — workers cut the grain, one drinks from a jug, others swim and nap in the shade. It is a summer so real you can almost feel the heat.

exploreAction.targetName: The Harvesters (1565) by Bruegel, Metropolitan Museum
exploreAction.instruction: The wheat field makes a diagonal wall of gold, and beyond it the land falls away to the sea. The workers rest, eat, swim — Bruegel painted work and its breaks as equally real. It is one panel of the lost series of the months, and the only one that survived complete.

name: The Tower of Babel — the small version (1563)
teaser: Bruegel painted the Tower twice — a large version in Vienna and this smaller one in Rotterdam. Both show the same ambition: a spiral city climbing toward a god that will not be reached.

exploreAction.targetName: The Tower of Babel — small version (1563) by Bruegel, Museum Boijmans
exploreAction.instruction: The tower's spiral ramps wind up into cloud — and the top is unfinished, already collapsing into mud and brick. The arched construction recalls the Colosseum; the message is the same as in the Vienna version: every empire builds its own ruin.

name: The Peasant Dance (1568)
teaser: Bruegel's village square erupts into dance — a bagpiper, a kissing couple, children, a table of drinkers. Nobody is painted as noble; everybody is painted as real.

exploreAction.targetName: The Peasant Dance (1568) by Bruegel, Kunsthistorisches Museum
exploreAction.instruction: The dancers move in a diagonal out of the painting — the piper leads, the couple in the center turns, the table tilts with drink. Bruegel painted the energy of a day off: loud, clumsy, and alive. The church looms behind; the dance is the sermon.

name: The Triumph of Death (1562)
teaser: Bruegel's armies of skeletons sweep across a landscape of burning houses, broken carts, and every rank of humanity — a painting of the plague years that still functions as the definitive memento mori.

exploreAction.targetName: The Triumph of Death (1562) by Bruegel, Prado
exploreAction.instruction: There is no center — death arrives from every side. A knight falls, a king is dragged from his throne, a musician plays on as the skeletons dance. Bruegel painted this during Europe's plague and war years; it is a mass grave with a frame.

name: Netherlandish Proverbs (1559)
teaser: Bruegel's village is a catalogue of over a hundred Dutch proverbs made literal — someone bangs his head against a brick wall, another sows seeds on the wind, a third has a roof of tiles missing from his head.

exploreAction.targetName: Netherlandish Proverbs (1559) by Bruegel, Gemäldegalerie Berlin
exploreAction.instruction: Treat it like a word-search: try to find 'armed to the teeth' (a man with a knife between his teeth), 'the world turned upside down' (a globe with a cross on top), 'to swim against the stream.' There are more than a hundred sayings hidden in the village.

name: The Fight Between Carnival and Lent (1559)
teaser: Bruegel's town square splits down the middle — Carnival's fat man jousts with a kitchen ladle against Lent's thin woman with a baker's peel. Gluttony and fasting face off while the town carries on.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fight Between Carnival and Lent (1559) by Bruegel, Kunsthistorisches Museum
exploreAction.instruction: Carnival, on the left, sits on a wine barrel with a roast pig at his feet; Lent, on the right, pulls a cart of fish and pretzels. The town between them is full of people being both. Bruegel painted the calendar as a perpetual argument between appetite and discipline.

name: The Wedding Dance in the Open Air (1566)
teaser: Bruegel's wedding party dances in a field — couples spinning, a bagpiper, a man trying to kiss a woman who is having none of it. Marriage as a loud, sweaty, joyful fact.

exploreAction.targetName: The Wedding Dance in the Open Air (1566) by Bruegel, Detroit Institute of Arts
exploreAction.instruction: Find the couple in the center mid-spin, and the woman in front of them laughing as her partner pulls her. The dancers' feet are off the ground — Bruegel painted motion so well the painting seems to sway. It is a portrait of a community at its most alive.

name: The Return of the Herd (1565)
teaser: Bruegel's cattle come down from the mountains as autumn darkens — the herd's slow descent mirrors the season's end. It is one of the surviving panels of his lost Months cycle.

exploreAction.targetName: The Return of the Herd (1565) by Bruegel, Kunsthistorisches Museum
exploreAction.instruction: The cows and oxen file down the slope, their horns silhouetted against a gray October sky. The trees are bare, the people carry wood, the year is closing. Bruegel painted the seasons as a farmer knows them — as work, weather, and time running out.

name: The Gloomy Day (1565)
teaser: Bruegel's early-spring painting — the sky is heavy, the trees bare, a village floods, and people struggle with the year's first work. Winter is over; so is the relief of winter.

exploreAction.targetName: The Gloomy Day (1565) by Bruegel, Kunsthistorisches Museum
exploreAction.instruction: The storm is breaking over the flooded valley while villagers work in the foreground. Bruegel's 'gloomy day' is March — the month of mud and no excuses. The painting is a portrait of a season that refuses to be cheerful.
